rounds.headline: At rest the panel called this studio-grade. Under the hand it was a five, and the same sentence came back from four seats independently: the gesture the whole direction exists for wrote a pixel and a count and left the date, the accessible name and the readout saying something else. One press put two moments on the same pixel; twenty put one seventy days past the wedding, outside the measure, silently. The editor declared an opaque ground and then re-declared it as a six per cent tint four lines later, so three rows of the plan printed straight through the panel in the state an owner lives in. Fifteen named, focus-ringed controls advertised verbs that did not exist, and the reversibility bar announced a change that had never happened and reversed nothing. Fifteen declarations written to make this work on a phone had never applied at any width, because a media query adds no specificity. Everything an owner touches was rebuilt: one writer of position, every fact derived from the date it produces, the editor moved into the rail, and the gate grown from 108 assertions to 262.

worst.problem: .b-edit declared background: var(--back) and re-declared background: var(--fore-06) four lines later in the same rule, so the editor plate computed to rgba(255,255,255,0.06). Three rows of the plan printed straight through it at 1440 and four at 390, with the steppers landing inside the word "fitting" — in the one state the owner spends their time in, in all three rooms.
worst.done: The plate is one opaque ground with the tint painted as a layer over it, and the editor no longer stands on the measure at all: at desk width it takes the rail beside the plan, and below that it is a sheet on the bottom edge of the screen. Two earlier attempts were rejected by their own refuters and both were right — a vertical band would have added twenty-five phantom days to the gap the owner is looking at, and a gutter inside the measure column starved the titles to 144px.

worst.problem: Every control on the owner surface except the four steppers was inert. Rows did not open, Done did not close, Escape did nothing, delete removed nothing, and the only way into the editing state was to edit the URL. The visible affordance was also the wrong object: the row was 520x79 and its only button was a 54x28 badge at the bottom of it.
worst.done: The row is the control — the badge stays as the visible mark and its hit area covers the row — and it opens on click, Enter and Space. Escape and Done close it and return focus to the row that opened it. Delete removes the moment and reflows the measure. Preview and Publish move the deck. Anything not built lost its button element and became inert text; the gate now fails on any button that does not do something.

worst.problem: One press of "move a week earlier" put the invitations on the same pixel as the menu tasting and the two rows printed as one unreadable smear. Twenty presses the other way placed an item at 149 days — seventy past the horizon the page is measured to, and 888px below the bottom of the measure — with the count still reading 79 and nothing said.
worst.done: place() is now the only thing that decides where an item sits, it runs after every change, and the move is clamped to the day itself with the steppers stating the ceiling rather than absorbing the press. Where two moments land close together the tick and the count stay on the true pixel and only the words are pushed clear, so the measure can never restate one item's distance as another's.

worst.problem: After a single press the row printed the count 16 beside its own date line reading SAT 8 AUG, its accessible name still said "in 23 days", and the readout dropped the calendar date permanently — so the owner moving a wedding milestone was never again told which date they had landed on. The readout collapsing from 347px to 99px also threw the button they were about to press again 209px sideways.
worst.done: setAway() is the single writer of an item's distance and derives one date, from which the count, the date line, the accessible name, the readout and the gap sentence are all rewritten in the same frame. The readout sits on its own line at a fixed measure, and the gate asserts the four stepper boxes are identical before and after every press.

worst.problem: The reversibility surface was a still life: it announced "the invitations moved seven days closer" into a live region before anything had been touched, never updated after a real move, and neither its button nor the Ctrl+Z printed beside it did anything. All five behaviour-gate assertions guarding it passed on an inert fragment with a disabled button.
worst.done: The bar is silent and inert until there is something true to say, then names the change that actually happened with the figure set like every other number on the page. Its button and the advertised key both restore the item and return focus to the control that made the change, and both stay out of the way of native undo inside a text field. The five assertions that certified a prop were replaced with ten that a prop cannot survive.

worst.problem: Fifteen declarations written to make this work on a phone had no effect at any width: every one was a bare class fighting a [data-medium] selector, and a media query adds no specificity. At 390 the field kept its 56px desk padding — 29% of the screen — under a comment reading "a desk padding on a phone is a quarter of the screen", the measure kept its 124px lane, and the printed page's own margins were dead at every width.
worst.done: The phone is now the base and the desk values live inside a min-width query, so the conflict is deleted rather than out-ranked. The two-column threshold moved from 901px to 1280px, where the measure genuinely has a column: at 901 it was still producing three collisions in a band neither gate had ever measured.

rounds.headline: The gesture held. Every seat that graded it said so, two of them in the same words, and the floor rose to 6.6 while Brand and Typography FELL — the panel looking harder at things it had passed. What it found was that the gesture was the only thing in the owner's panel that had been built. The create verb opened the editor on somebody else's moment. The title field, on a surface whose whole subject is a person's own words, discarded everything typed into it. Delete removed a moment with no way back, dropped focus to the body, killed the advertised key for the rest of the session, and left the reversibility bar offering to restore a row that no longer existed — an offer that, pressed, restored nothing and cleared itself as though it had worked. The bar itself rendered a thousand pixels below the button that filled it. The publish ceremony carried two buttons and neither did anything, on the screen the product exists for. And three of the 262 gate assertions were tautologies, one of them covering that live defect. Everything an owner can now do joins one history stack with its own undo closure; the gate went to 357 assertions and learned to grade placeholders and the tracking ladder.

worst.problem: The owner's only creation verb created nothing: "Add a moment" opened the editor on the first existing moment with its title pre-filled, and the title field wrote nowhere, so there was no path in the whole direction by which an owner could put a new moment on the plan or name one.
worst.done: Add builds a real moment, inserts it in date order, opens the panel on it with an empty focused field, and joins the history so Ctrl+Z removes it. The title field writes through to the record, the row, the word-safe trim and the accessible name, and a rename is itself undoable. A refuter caught that the first version of this fix would have thrown on the new row, because the editor resolves its record through the fixture.

worst.problem: Delete was the one destructive act on the surface and the only action outside the reversibility system that already guarded a one-day move. It dropped focus to the body, which — because the key handler was bound to the field — killed the advertised Ctrl+Z for the rest of the session, and the bar kept a live offer to undo the move before it.
worst.done: Every change now carries its own undo closure on one stack, and undo peeks before it pops, so a press that cannot restore anything no longer clears the bar as though it had. Delete keeps the live node rather than its markup — the owner's edits live on the DOM, so rebuilding from the record would have restored a moment they never had — puts focus on the next row, and the key handler moved to the document.

worst.problem: The move is the one animated thing in the product, and below 1280 it happened off screen: the edited row opened 152px below the fold with the sheet covering the lower half of the phone, so the owner pressed, every fact updated correctly, and they saw nothing move.
worst.done: The row is scrolled into the band between the top of the screen and the sheet, on open and after any press that would take it out — gated on the sheet being a sheet rather than on a width, so where the editor is the static rail the scroll path is unreachable and the page keeps its place exactly as round 1 asserted. The sheet now reserves its own band in layout, so the last rows can no longer be stranded under it at maximum scroll.

worst.problem: Three of the 262 assertions were true by construction: one whose predicate was a literal tautology, one whose exemption list emptied its own array, and one whose else branch restated its if. The second was covering a live defect — the two publish buttons — because its state loop never visited that state.
worst.done: The trim assertion tests a word boundary rather than a prefix. The dead-control check now presses every button in seven states and requires the page, the state or the focus to change, so a control that does nothing fails by construction. The sheet assertion asserts what the sheet owes instead of restating its own condition.

worst.problem: The wedding morning was the worst-written screen in the set: it printed the fact it exists for twice, closed on a cancelled hotel search, and carried an eleven-week-old timestamp. The count — the whole composition on every other screen — was demoted to a 12px micro-label while the couple's name was promoted into the display register.
worst.done: The morning states its one fact once, drops the stamp, names how you got here rather than what did not happen, and the arrived countdown takes the count's own slot at the display step. Two refuters disagreed about whether to delete the closing line; the one that measured the screen won, and it stayed.

worst.problem: The tracking ladder was declared and then applied by hand, so it did not hold: 24px sans rendered at two different letterfits, 30px at two more, eight prose blocks carried no tracking at all, and every size raised at desk width kept the phone's tracking.
worst.done: Every font-size in the file now carries its step on the same rule, and the ladder is enforced mechanically: audit.mjs grades it, failing when one family at one size renders at two letterfits anywhere in the state matrix. Two sizes moved so the ladder is unambiguous — the ceremonial label is a step up in size as well as tracking, and a share token is data, not a label.

rounds.headline: The floor rose from 6.6 to 7.2 and the panel turned on the half of the product it had barely graded. Six of the seven seats said a version of the same thing: the owner's fifteen seconds are finished, and everything the owner hands over is not. Preview previewed a different plan from the one on screen - an added moment vanished, a moment marked Hidden was still listed, and Back to the plan destroyed the edit in silence - because every state remounted from a load-time snapshot and the control titled "What guests see" wrote to a DOM attribute and nothing else. The record room and the printed keepsake, whose entire subject is the past, showed none of it: a CSS rule took the disclosure away and took the heading, the count and every row with it, and the one assertion guarding that surface PASSED by proving the control was gone. The reversibility bar, moved into the editor last round, had no positioned ancestor at the owner's own two widths and painted across the 148px count. And the measured gate could not see the ground it was grading: a page whose ground is a composited wash reported white, so an invisible way out of the preview scored clean. Both gates were rebuilt around what they had missed - the contrast check now composites the real ground, tracking and leading are read off the page and enforced against it, <summary> counts as a control, and the behaviour gate went from 357 assertions to 424.

worst.problem: The record room and the printed keepsake showed none of the past. [data-past="listed"] hid the <summary>, and because the heading and the count lived inside it they were deleted too; the two rules meant to compensate were inert, because Chromium hides a closed <details> through ::details-content and display on a child cannot override it. Driven at 1440, zero of three rows passed checkVisibility. The gate's only assertion for that surface passed by proving the control was gone - the very thing causing the loss.
worst.done: Where the past is listed there is now no disclosure at all: the renderer emits a plain head and the rows, and print forces it whichever room made the sheet. The two dead CSS rules are gone. Four assertions replaced the one, over both rooms at print, desk and phone, requiring every row to pass checkVisibility, the heading to be visible, the count to equal the rows rendered, and no <summary> to exist where nothing folds.

worst.problem: At 1280 and 1440 the reversibility bar painted on top of the count. The bar is absolutely positioned inside the editor, and the rule that puts the editor in the rail reset it to position: static, so there was no positioned ancestor and the bar escaped to the sticky column - landing at (202, 83-153) across a numeral occupying 106-233, and taking the pointer there too. The editor meanwhile held 78px of reserve the bar never entered. Below 1280 the sheet was correct, which is why every phone frame looked right.
worst.done: position: relative with inset: auto, so the panel sits exactly where static put it and the bar lands in its own reserved band, raised to 88px against a measured 85px. A refuter caught that relative alone would have reactivated the base rule's fixed offsets and shifted the panel 12px out of its column. Eight assertions now require the bar to sit inside the editor and never to intersect the count, at four widths.

worst.problem: Press Hidden and the row, its badge and its accessible name all said hidden; press Preview, three hundred pixels away, and the guest still saw it. Visibility was written to a DOM attribute only, the fixture's live list was a snapshot taken at load, and every state remounts from the fixture - so a moment added never reached a guest, a moment deleted came back, and Back to the plan silently destroyed the owner's work. Six assertions covered the toggle and every one of them stopped at the owner's own DOM.
worst.done: The record is the store. add, delete, the date and the visibility toggle all write through to it, the derived lists are computed on call rather than once at load, and the guest lists are filtered in one place by one flag - so an owner still sees what they hid and a guest does not. Three cross-state assertions now carry an edit through Preview and back.

worst.problem: Delete threw the page up to 638px away with no motion connecting the two positions, and undo restored the moment without restoring the place, so the way back left the owner exactly as lost. The cause was focus: the browser scrolls to whatever takes it, and the row that inherited focus after a removal was handed it plainly. The behaviour gate never saw it - it visited 390, 768, 1280 and 1440, and the worst of it is at 320 and 1024.
worst.done: One function hands focus over and it never moves the page: preventScroll everywhere, then a nudge only where the target is genuinely off screen, using the same band math the editor already had. Every history entry records the view it happened at and undo restores it. The gate now drives delete and undo at 320, 768, 1024 and 1280 and measures the picture on screen rather than the scroll offset, because removing a row changes the document height and the browser's own scroll anchoring moves scrollY by design.

worst.problem: Two thirds of a calendar broke in half in the record. The date lane is a hard 76px and an 11px mono uppercase date at 0.16em needs about 84px, so SAT 18 APR, SAT 22 AUG, SAT 29 AUG and SAT 19 SEP all wrapped, severing the weekday from the day it belongs to and leaving the rows alternating 39px and 55px. It was invisible in every shot because the disclosure is closed by default, and invisible to the tracking gate because the letterfit was correct - the lane was simply too narrow for it.
worst.done: 96px and nowrap, so a future overrun is a visible collision the gate can catch rather than a silent second line, and the leading joins the ladder. Two assertions drive the open disclosure at 390 in both rooms and require every date box to be a single line.

worst.problem: The gate could not see the ground it was grading. This lab paints its page ground as an opaque colour plus a composited wash - a deliberate decision, documented twice - and the contrast check walked backgroundColor only, so everything outside the artifact was measured against white while the pixels were ink. A live control was hiding behind it: the strip carrying the owner's only way out of a preview was written in literal ink on the ink ground, 1:1, and passed in every room. The tracking check had the matching hole - it compared each family and size only with itself, so a seventh undeclared value could ship clean.
worst.done: The backdrop composites single-colour gradients and reports anything else as unmeasured rather than guessing. The preview strip is painted from the fore ladder, as is the lab's own caption, which had the same defect. Both ladders are now read off the page and enforced against it, and leading joined tracking as a declared, graded axis - six steps, bound by role, with sixty hand-set values routed onto them.

rounds.headline: The floor rose again, 7.2 to 7.5, and four seats rose by half a point or more - but the round belongs to one sentence five of the seven seats wrote independently: the wedding morning is a title card. The best idea in the direction, real days at real distance, was absent from the one screen the whole company is judged by; the past opened there into a flat dated table, and a second moment dated on the wedding day made the wedding itself vanish from its own screen. Underneath it the measured seat found the countdown had no arrival branch and no plural: a wedding one day out rendered "1 DAYS" at ninety-six pixels, the morning "0 DAYS", the week after "-6 DAYS", on every guest surface and on the card that lands in the chat - and the assertion written to guard it could not see it, because CSS uppercases the unit. The venue a guest is told to go to was a string literal typed into the renderer twice, from a record that has no venue field. The link card announced neither its figure nor its date to a screen reader, and painted its own ground from a ladder a rasterised asset can never follow - white on white in one room, ink on ink in another. The past said the same thing twice wherever round 3 had opened it. And nothing in the product answered a press: eight hover rules, zero active rules, and on a phone the only acknowledgement was the browser's own tap highlight, an unowned fourth hue nobody chose. The morning now draws its past in the product's own language at two pixels a day; the countdown has one owner and three states; leading is bound to its role and space has a declared ladder. The behaviour gate went 424 to 454 assertions.

worst.problem: The wedding morning was 206 characters, one control, and a 715px card against 1674px in the received artifact: the measure - the whole thesis of the direction - was absent on the one day it is about, and its past opened into a flat dated table. Five of the seven seats raised it independently.
worst.done: The morning draws its past in the product's own language: the same rail, the same ticks, the same mono date beside the person's words, running downward from today into the closed months at two pixels a day, headed "days back" and carrying no accent, because nothing behind you is the next thing. No new data, no new control, and the same place() that positions what is ahead positions what is behind. Two refuters shaped it: a completed forward measure would have spanned 3,300 pixels with two hundred-day voids, and inverting the screen would have duplicated the rail's own origin under the display word.

worst.problem: The countdown had no arrival branch and no plural. Driven, not read: a wedding one day out renders "1 DAYS" at 96px on a phone and 148px at a desk, the morning renders "0 DAYS", a week after renders "-6 DAYS", and the card that lands in the chat does the same. The fixture already carried an accessor written for exactly this, and the two biggest numbers in the design were the only ones that never called it. The guarding assertion could not fail: CSS uppercases the unit, so the page says "1 DAYS" while the regex looks for "1 days".
worst.done: One owner for the clock, answering with a state rather than a string, because the three cases are three compositions: a figure and its unit while the day is ahead, the word the morning is already built on when it arrives, and a sentence with no numeral once it has gone. A guest can no longer be shown a negative. Graded at two days out, one day out, the day itself and three days past, reading the figure and the unit as separate elements because innerText cannot see this.

worst.problem: A second moment dated on the wedding day made the wedding itself vanish from its own screen: the morning rendered only the first item on the clock, and anything else dated that day was in neither the ahead list nor the behind list, so it existed nowhere. Reached by typing a date the editor itself accepts.
worst.done: The morning names everything dated on it, ordered explicitly rather than by fixture order, and heads the block "Happening today" when it holds more than one. Asserted against the record rather than against a literal: every live moment dated on the clock must appear in the text of the screen.

worst.problem: The unfurl card painted its ground from the fore ladder, so the one artifact that gets rasterised and lands in somebody else's chat client followed a room it can never be in: white on white in the paper room, and #111 on #111 on the publish screen, where the owner previews what lands in the message. Separately its accessible name replaced its own contents, so the 64px figure and the date were announced to nobody.
worst.done: The card has one ground, written in fixed tokens that are still on the palette, and it is shown on a hairline plate wherever it is previewed. Its name is built from what it shows, and it now says when the figure was true - a chat client caches a preview at the moment it is sent, and the bubble beside it promises the plan updates itself.

worst.problem: Nothing in the product answered a press: eight hover rules and zero active rules, so on a phone - where hover does not exist - the primary gesture had no acknowledgement at all until the sheet arrived, and the only thing marking a touch was the browser's own tap highlight, an unowned teal nobody chose and nothing overrode.
worst.done: State here is ink density, so a press is one step denser than a hover, declared after the hover rules so equal specificity cannot lose, with the tap highlight taken off the controls that now own their own press. No motion work needed: the reduced-motion block already zeroes every transition, and a colour step is state rather than motion.

worst.problem: The venue - the only fact telling a guest where to go - was a string literal typed into the renderer in two places and presented as a fact about the record, which has no venue field. The gate proved it by matching the same literal.
worst.done: Removed rather than invented: a place field is a data-model change and out of scope, and writing one into the fixture would be exactly the hand-rolled data the brief forbids. The milestone titles that genuinely name the venue are real record content and are untouched. The gate now asserts the page does NOT claim a venue.
